1.goal: To say, in one sentence, that the three previous lessons arrive together today.
1.interaction: T–S, one line from you and straight on.
run: THIS LESSON CLOSES THE BLOCK. Reread the records of the three previous ones before you start: they are what steers the planning of the next lessons.
Say it once, and only once: the room is a simulation, and nobody in it has better English than she does. Group shame is her real obstacle — naming it once helps; repeating it does not.
exact: This room is a simulation. Nobody here has better English than you. Today you go in.
1.support: If she asks who will be there, say four people and move.
1.challenge: Ask which of the four she expects to speak to first.
1.monitoring: Whether naming the obstacle settles her or raises it. Once is the dose.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The sample starts at stage 3.
1.transition: Move on when she is on the next screen.

2.goal: The room: four people and a clock.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the card on screen together.
run: Read the card with her.
Confirm two things: there are four people, and nobody is going to say her name.
Do not anticipate the Q&A question. The lesson depends on her not seeing it.
2.expected: That she knows who she wants to ask what, before the call starts.
2.support: If the three blur together, ask what each of them does that she does not.
2.challenge: Ask which of the three she would rather not have to interrupt.
2.monitoring: Whether she is already choosing a question. That is the work starting early, and it is welcome.
2.evidence: Who she wants to ask, and about what.
2.transition: Move on when she knows who she wants to ask what.

3.goal: The minute with NO model and no preparation. This attempt is half the evidence of the day.
3.interaction: S speaks for one minute; you time it and say nothing.
run: Give the instruction below and start.
Call the time out loud only at the end.
DO NOT CORRECT AND DO NOT SUGGEST. Not before, not during.
exact: One minute: who are you, and what do you do?
3.expected: Whatever she has. Twenty seconds is a legitimate result, and it IS the data.
3.support: None here. Anything you add contaminates the baseline.
3.challenge: None here, for the same reason.
3.monitoring: How many sentences came out, whether what is new this year appeared, and whether she apologized for her English.
3.evidence: The three notes above. They are half the evidence of the block.
3.transition: Move on when she finishes — even at twenty seconds.

4.goal: To show an introduction that works, AFTER her own attempt.
4.interaction: S marks on screen; T–S on the two CCQs.
run: The four sentences on screen. She marks the three things the introduction does.
If she apologized for her English at stage 3, this is where that is dealt with — once, without a lecture.
exact: What is the last sentence for? (To give them something to ask about.)
And why not explain the doctorate? (Because it gives nobody a question.)
4.expected: Three things marked: who she is, what she does, and what is new this year.
4.support: If the third one resists, ask which sentence she would ask a question about.
4.challenge: Ask her to write a fourth sentence of her own that gives someone a question.
4.monitoring: Whether she treats the last sentence as decoration. It is the one that keeps the conversation going.
4.evidence: Whether the apology appeared, and whether it went away when named.
4.transition: Move on when the three are marked.

5.goal: For her to find what the three good answers have in common.
5.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S on the pattern.
run: She marks the three. Then ask what the three she chose DO.
exact: What do the three you chose DO?
5.expected: The answer you want, from her: the three DO something — they ask, they answer what she knows, or they hand the turn back. The others close the door politely.
5.support: If the pattern will not come, read one good and one closing answer back to back and ask which one leaves something to say next.
5.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the closing answers into one that keeps her in.
5.monitoring: Whether she reads politeness as the goal. Politeness is what closes the door here.
5.evidence: Whether she names the pattern herself.
5.transition: Move on when she names the pattern.

6.goal: The four moves said out loud.
6.interaction: T throws the situation; S answers with the move. Four, fast.
run: You throw the situation, she answers with the move. Fast, four times.
Correction here is immediate. After this nothing is corrected until the feedback.
CLOSE THE CARD AND THE MOVES ON THE SCREEN before round one.
6.expected: Four answers, each using one of the moves.
6.support: If a move will not come, give the first three words and let her finish.
6.challenge: Throw a situation where two moves would work and ask which she chose.
6.monitoring: Whether the move arrives before she starts explaining herself.
6.evidence: How many of the four come out without the screen.
6.transition: Move on when the four have come out.

7.goal: The production of the block: one minute, two questions asked uninvited, and one unforeseen question answered.
7.interaction: Role-play. You play all four parts and do not leave them.
run: One minute of her introduction.
Then the conversation goes on between Marta, Paulo and Sofia — and nobody says her name. She has to come in and ask two questions.
Then play Sofia's recorded question, ONCE. If she asks for it again, play it again and count it as a hit: it is the move from lesson 10.
If she waits out the whole two minutes without coming in, that is the finding of the block. Note it and do not rescue her.
Record everything.
7.expected: One minute, two questions asked without being invited, and an answer to the question she did not see.
7.support: If she freezes on Sofia's question, replay it once, unchanged, and wait.
7.challenge: Let the conversation run thirty seconds longer and see whether a third question comes.
7.monitoring: Whether she comes in without being called, and whether she asks for the recorded question to be repeated.
7.evidence: The recording, plus whether she came in uninvited. It is the central finding of the block.
7.transition: Move on when she has answered the unforeseen question.

8.goal: To hand back three points and one number, out loud.
8.interaction: T–S, three points and one measurement.
run: Three points: one that worked, one that did not, and ONE measurement said out loud (how many questions she asked, or how long the introduction lasted).
If she came in without being called, say it in as many words. It is the thing she said she cannot do.
Do not add new content. Round two is the same introduction, shorter.
exact: Nobody called your name, and you came in anyway. That is the thing you told me you cannot do.
8.expected: Three points she recognizes, and one number she had not heard before.
8.support: If she dismisses the achievement, play the ten seconds where she came in.
8.challenge: Ask her to say, before round two, which of the three she intends to change.
8.monitoring: Whether the point about coming in lands as a result or as a detail. It is not a detail.
8.evidence: The three points and the number. They go in the block record.
8.transition: Move on when the three points are on the board.

9.goal: The introduction only, in thirty seconds, to someone already leaving the room.
run: Thirty seconds, the introduction only, to someone who is already on their way out.
Record this one too. The two recordings from today close the block file.
9.expected: Thirty seconds with what is new this year still in them.
9.support: If she cannot cut, ask which sentence gives the other person a question.
9.challenge: Ask for it once more in fifteen seconds and see which sentence survives.
9.monitoring: What she cuts. If what is new this year goes, what is left is a job title — and it is the new thing that gives the other person a question.
9.evidence: The second recording, and what she cut.
9.transition: Move on when the thirty seconds are up.

10.goal: To close the block out loud, and to record the two answers the next planning starts from.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close of the block.
run: She ticks what she recognizes.

CLOSE THE BLOCK WITH HER, OUT LOUD: four lessons, four recordings, and the first question of hers in English on record in this course. She has abandoned eight courses — naming what changed is not kindness, it is what makes the ninth different.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has her introduction recorded and the written answer to today's question.
Announce block 2: following a group discussion, not just an introduction.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If the close feels thin, play ten seconds of the lesson-9 recording next to today's.
10.challenge: Ask when the next Meteoro meeting is, and which of the four moves she takes into it.
10.monitoring: Whether she hears the four recordings as progress or as four attempts. Only one of the two readings keeps her in the course.
10.evidence: BLOCK RECORD, filled before you close: did she come into the conversation without being called? how much did she understand without asking for translation, compared with lesson 10? The planning of the next lessons starts from those two answers.
10.transition: Close the lesson, and the block.
